Greece Man arrested after Scottish woman found dead inside suitcase in Athens Greek police say 26-year-old Afghan national is believed to have left Elisabeth-Jane Ross’s body in derelict building Helena Smith in Athens Sun 2 Aug 2026 14.29 EDT First published on Sun 2 Aug 2026 10.56 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Greek authorities have arrested an Afghan national in connection with the death of a Scottish woman whose body was found in a suitcase in an abandoned building in central Athens. Elisabeth-Jane Ross, 38, a charity worker described as an “angel full of innocence and goodness” by friends, had been in Greece for almost three weeks when she is believed to have died. Police sources said the suspect was a 26-year-old Afghan citizen who had allegedly confessed to the crime. He had been brought in for questioning by Greece’s homicide division last Thursday, two days after Ross’s body was publicly identified. A statement released by police on Sunday said: “A criminal file has been opened against a 26-year-old foreign national for intentional homicide, robbery and violation of the law [regarding] weapons.” Explaining the accusation of ownership of illegal weapons, security officials said “various arms – some real, some fake” had been discovered in the suspect’s home, also thought to be in the downtown area of Kypseli where the body was discovered. He is expected to be charged on Monday. Throughout the investigation, Greek authorities had worked closely with the UK’s National Crime Agency (NCA) and Police Scotland, according to the statement. Ross, who had strong links with the charity sector in Greece, is the daughter of a prominent lawyer in Edinburgh, where she also lived. She was reported to have friends in Kypseli, where her body was discovered on 18 July by a homeless man in what had once been a car park. Wrapped in cloth, it had been placed in a suitcase left in a decrepit, rubbish-strewn building at the site. Sources told the Guardian that the suspect’s alleged use of credit cards that belonged to Ross had contributed to police identifying him. “He was caught on camera withdrawing money with the cards from various ATMs,” one said. “The credit cards belonged to Ms Ross. That played a big role in leading us to him.” For days, investigators were unable to make headway, citing the lack of fingerprints or DNA on the suitcase. Adding to the mystery was the discovery that her mobile phone had been used until the time when the body was publicly identified last week. Police had described text messages sent to her father and other members of her family as deliberately misleading. The messages had spoken of her “need to be alone”. The Briton’s “dispersed movements” in the days leading up to her death had made the quest to track her killer even harder. After leaving the home of close friends in Keratsini, a suburb close to the port of Piraeus, where she had stayed for two weeks after flying to Greece, she had gone her own way, renting an apartment in the district of Exarchia in downtown Athens. Greek media outlets reported the suspect had been found in possession of the keys to the rental apartment and that he was “the partner” of one of the Briton’s friends. “As confirmed, the victim arrived in the country on June 26 and stayed at the home of friends until July 10, from where she departed to an unknown [address],” the police statement said. The homicide division said it had made the announcement after amassing evidence that proved the Afghan had “placed the body in the case and carried it to the abandoned car park” in Kypseli. Analysis of CCTV footage had played a role. “The subsequent preliminary investigation … using investigative material and digital analysis of video footage, proved the involvement of the 26-year-old foreign national in the incident. [He] was brought in [for questioning] on 30 July and confessed to his actions,” the statement said. It remains unknown how Ross died. Media reports quoted the suspect as telling police that when he visited the flat in Exarchia he had discovered her lifeless body in the bathroom. An initial on-site postmortem showed there were no evident signs of injury or struggle on the Briton’s body but proved inconclusive because of advanced decomposition. Authorities have fast-tracked toxicological tests and analysis of vital organ tissues to determine the cause of death. Grigoris Leon, who heads the Hellenic Society of Forensic Medicine, told the Guardian that examination of the lungs and eyes would help provide answers and determine “whether she had died a natural death”. As tributes have poured in, flowers have been left beside the abandoned lot in Kypseli. One note read: “Here lies an angel.” One friend in Edinburgh agreed with that, saying: “We have lost an angel, an angel full of innocence and goodness who only wanted to help people wherever she went.”The UK Foreign Office previously said: “Our thoughts are with Elisabeth’s family during this difficult time. We are providing consular support and are in contact with the local authorities.” A Police Scotland spokesperson said: “We are aware of the death of a Scottish woman in Athens and are liaising with authorities in Greece. Officers are providing support to her family in Scotland.” Explore more on these topics Greece Scotland Europe news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://www.dw.com/en/argentina-s-milei-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NRXn Milei spoke at the UN General Assembly in New York days before threatening international legal action against the UK (FILE: 23/09/2026) Image: CNP/AdMedia/picture alliance Advertisement Argentine President Javier Milei on Monday gave the United Kingdom two weeks to halt an oil project near the Falkland Islands or face international legal action. The potentially lucrative project has intensified the long-running sovereignty dispute as the islands prepare for oil production that could transform their small economy. What has Argentina threatened to do? Milei said Argentina would take the dispute to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea in Hamburg if the UK did not halt the Sea Lion project within two weeks. "I instructed the Foreign Ministry and our legal teams to initiate arbitration proceedings against the United Kingdom for the illegal sacking of our resources through the Sea Lion Project in the North Falklands Basin," Milei wrote on X. "If within two weeks the United Kingdom does not stop the illegitimate exploitation, we will go to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea," he added. Argentina argues that Britain's authorization of oil exploration violates a UN resolution calling on both sides to refrain from unilateral actions while their sovereignty dispute remains unresolved. Port Stanley is the capital of the British-controlled Falkland Islands, which Argentina claims as the Malvinas (FILE: 07/10/2019) Image: Pablo Porciuncula/AFP Milei has also threatened to bar companies involved in unauthorized oil exploration around the Falklands from operating in Argentina's oil and mining sectors. His government has sent Argentina's Congress a bill proposing prison terms of up to 20 years for extracting resources around the islands without Argentine authorization. Argentine authorities say they are investigating at least 60 companies and executives for possible violations. What is the Sea Lion oil project? Sea Lion is a major offshore oil field around 220 kilometers (137 miles) north of the Falkland Islands. The project is being developed by Israel's Navitas Petroleum and Britain's Rockhopper Exploration under licenses issued by the Falkland Islands authorities. Oil production is expected to begin in 2028. The companies have rejected Argentina's objections, saying they hold valid licenses for the project. Britain and Argentina fought a 10-week war over the Falkland Islands in 1982 after Argentine forces invaded the British-controlled territory [FILE: 1982] Image: PA/empics/dpa/picture alliance The UK has also defended the right of the Falkland Islanders to develop their natural resources. Why are the Falkland Islands disputed? The Falkland Islands have been under British control since 1833, but Argentina claims sovereignty over the archipelago, which it calls the Malvinas. Argentina invaded the islands in 1982, triggering a 10-week war with the UK. The conflict killed 649 Argentine military personnel, 255 British service members and three islanders before British forces retook the territory. The UK says the islanders have the right to determine their own future. In a 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters backed remaining a British Overseas Territory, with turnout of about 92%. Argentina rejects the referendum and maintains its sovereignty claim. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c862.text: Image source, Sameer AL-DOUMY / AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Students carried out a blocking protest at a secondary school in Lille By Henry Moore Published 17 minutes ago More than 400 people, mostly minors, were detained in France on Tuesday over student protests at high schools across the country, the French interior minister said. The demonstrations, which began in Paris and have seen teenagers blockade their schools for days, stem from issues including overcrowded classes and teacher shortages. At least 10 teachers and several students, as well as 48 law enforcement officials, were injured during Tuesday's protests, officials said. According to the education ministry, at least 400 schools were affected. Pictures and videos appeared to show bins being set alight and bus stops damaged by protesters. "We're here to deliver a message," one 16-year-old female student told the AFP news agency. "We're not here to smash everything up for no reason. We're here precisely to say that the education system is completely broken. There are 34 of us in each class, and it's just not feasible. The teachers are overworked." Taking to X, French Education Minister Ãdouard Geffray said students have the right to protest, but condemned reports of violence as "indefensible". Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez told BFMTV 440 people were detained, adding: "We don't have the final tally yet, but I'm told two thirds led to police custody." French media reported that protesters hurled projectiles at police, who responded with batons and tear gas. Speaking to AFP, Ryad Rani, president of Union Syndicale LycÃ©enne, which represents students, accused the French government of "repression" and police of using excessive force. When pressed on the police response to the protests, which has been criticised by several French politicians, NuÃ±ez said it had been "carried out in an extremely proportionate manner". Writing on social media on Tuesday evening, education minister Geffray said: "The right to demonstrate is a fundamental freedom that cannot serve as an excuse for such actions. "To legitimise them or, in this context, to call for extending the blockades is to endanger our students as well as public employees. It is irresponsible." Image source, Reuters Image caption, French students blocked the entrance to a high school in Paris The movement at French lycÃ©es, equivalent to sixth form in the UK or high school in the US, began last week in the Ãle-de-France region around Paris. On Monday, France's Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu warned any escalation in the student protests would be "irresponsible" following the arrest of 164 people. Lecornu cited reported incidents at protests in a post on X, saying: "Fireworks, fires, violence near high schools: nothing justifies endangering students, staff, or police officers." The continuing student demonstrations on Tuesday coincided with nationwide walkouts by unions representing teachers, hospital staff and civil servants to protest against issues including low wages and working conditions. NuÃ±ez said these protests, with at least 200,000 participants reported, mostly went without incident. https://www.dw.com/en/prague-honors-roma.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OW7L Since the end of WWII, the role of Roma resistance fighters was largely unknown Image: Luboš Palata/DW Advertisement For more than half a million Roma in Czechia and Slovakia , October 15, 2026, marks an important milestone. That day, an exhibition on a largely forgotten chapter of Czech history opened at the Museum of the Romani National Revival in Prague. The exhibit explores the role of Czech and Slovak Romani resistance fighters during the Nazi German occupation and the dismantling of Czechoslovakia from 1938 to 1945. Until now, Czech and Slovak Roma appeared in the history of World War II almost exclusively as victims of the Holocaust against Roma and Sinti. In the so-called Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia, Nazi Germany murdered approximately 90% of the Czech Roma during World War II. However, what is less well known is that a large number of Czech and Slovak Roma fought against the German occupiers as partisans in resistance groups and as soldiers in the Czechoslovak Underground Army, or Defense of the Nation, ON. The organizers of the exhibition hope that people will bring their children and grandchildren to show that Roma and Sinti have their own heroes Image: Luboš Palata/DW Roma have heroes, too The exhibition at the Museum of the Roma National Movement therefore marks a turning point in how the Roma are viewed during World War II . At least that is the hope of museum director Emil Scuka, a lawyer, former prosecutor and one of the best-known Czech Roma activists. "We were not only victims; we were also heroes," Scuka said in his speech to several hundred attendees at the exhibition opening, most of whom were Roma from Czechia and Slovakia. "Many people, not even among the Roma themselves, are aware that we Roma fought against Nazism," he noted. In his view, "organizing and opening the exhibition was something my generation owed to these Roma heroes and today we are repaying that debt." Scuka called on those present: "Bring your children and grandchildren here so they can see for themselves and realize that the Roma have heroes too!" He also pointed out that this topic had been completely marginalized in Czech and Slovak historical writing for decades and that the Roma had therefore decided on their own to document the fates of their war heroes. The exhibition presents the detailed life stories of 100 of the most significant Roma partisans and Roma soldiers from the Czech underground army and resistance groups who fought against the Nazis. "We found over 1,400 Romani fighters in the archives. From among them, we selected the 100 most interesting stories for this exhibition," said exhibition curator Radoslav Scuka at the opening. Unseen heroes — Sinti and Roma resist Nazis To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Groundbreaking research on Roma resistance fighters Among these figures is Anton Facuna, a sergeant in the American intelligence agency Office of Strategic Services (OSS), who was flown to Slovakia in October 1944 on a secret mission. Slovakia had been a puppet state of Hitler from 1939 to 1945. Another is Josef Serinek, known by the nickname "Black Partisan from Vysocina," who managed to escape from the Nazi concentration camp for Roma in Lety and subsequently founded and commanded the large Capajev-Cerny partisan unit in the Bohemian-Moravian Highlands. In 2022, Czech President Milos Zeman posthumously awarded him the Medal for Heroism. Toward the end of his life, Serinek shared his memories with historian Jan Tesar, who later wrote the three-volume book "Ceska cikanska rapsodie", which translates to Czech Gypsy Rhapsody. Except for Tesar's book, the history of Roma resistance against Nazism has not been researched by Czech and Slovak historians to this day. "I am not aware of any scholarly historical work that deals with Roma resistance against Nazism," Prokop Tomek, a historian at the Military History Institute in Prague , told DW. "The number of 1,400 Roma who took part in the fight against Nazism as members of the resistance or in the foreign army does not strike me as an exaggeration and corresponds to the proportion of the Roma population in Czechoslovakia," Tomek said, adding that the "exhibition on the Roma resistance against Nazism during the war is undoubtedly groundbreaking." The life of resistance fighter Anton Facuna is one of around 100 examples on display Image: Luboš Palata/DW Fears of revealing one's Roma identity To this day, many Roma in Czechia and Slovakia do not publicly acknowledge their ethnic identity. This is partly due to experiences with the Holocaust during the Nazi era that have been passed down through generations. Czech historians and politicians continue to debate the extent to which the Czech authorities of the Protectorate were complicit in the extermination of the Czech Roma. However, one thing is certain: the police registration of all Roma, which had been enshrined in law in Czechoslovakia since 1927, facilitated the extermination of the Roma by the German Nazis. According to estimates by the Czech government, approximately 250,000 Roma live in the country today. In the 2021 census, however, only 21,000 people identified as Roma. Of all ethnic groups in Czechia, which has a population of 10 million, the Roma are among the three largest ethnic minorities in terms of numbers. However, they are the most socially disadvantaged, have very little political representation, and are therefore scarcely present in Czech politics.
